sections.overview: The Longlure Frogfish is a bottom-living ambush predator of the tropical western Atlantic, especially Caribbean reefs. It often perches among sponges, where its shape, color and skin texture help it disappear against the background.
sections.identification: Its short, globular body has a huge upward-facing mouth, rough scaleless skin, and pectoral fins with elbow-like joints that resemble little legs. Dark, pale-ringed ocelli occur on the body and fins; the pattern is more useful for identification than its highly variable background color, which may be red, yellow, brown, green, or nearly white. FishBase reports a maximum total length of 20 cm. DORIS gives a 7–20 cm range without specifying the measurement convention; reliable weight, body-height, body-width, or sex-specific size measurements were not found. Its first dorsal spine forms a fishing rod about 21–32% of standard length, roughly twice the second spine, and ends in a flattened, flag-like lure.
sections.habitat: It lives on tropical reefs and is commonly found around sponges. Its range includes Bermuda, Florida, the Gulf of Mexico, the Bahamas and Caribbean islands, then south along the western Atlantic coast toward northern South America. FishBase records it to 66 m, though it is usually encountered in shallow water.
sections.diet: It feeds mainly on fishes and also takes mobile crustaceans such as shrimps and crabs.
sections.behavior: It relies on camouflage and ambush rather than chasing prey across the reef, remaining nearly motionless until a small animal approaches.
sections.reproduction: It is oviparous and its eggs are released in a floating gelatinous ribbon or mass known as an egg raft; the larvae are pelagic.
sections.ecology: The Dwarf Frogfish (A. pauciradiatus) is a close regional comparison: it rarely exceeds 5 cm and is usually pale yellow with few markings.
sections.conservation: FishBase reports the species as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List, based on an assessment dated 2013.
